title: Comments of Rehmana Younis on Large AI Data Center Loads and Continuous Reliability Decision-Making under AD26-8.

​UNITED STATES OF AMERICA​
                    ​BEFORE THE FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION​


                                   ​Commissioner-led Reliability Technical Conference​
                                                     ​Docket No. AD26-8-000​


            ​COMMENTS​​OF​​REHMANA​​YOUNIS​​ON​​LARGE​​AI​​DATA​​CENTER​​LOADS​
            ​AND CONTINUOUS RELIABILITY DECISION-MAKING​


              I​ ​ ​respectfully​ ​submit​ ​these​ ​comments​ ​in​ ​connection​ ​with​ ​the​ ​Commission’s​ ​October​ ​21,​ ​2026​
 ​reliability​ ​technical​​conference.​​The​​discussion​​of​​growing​​electricity​​demand​​from​​AI​​data​​centers​​raises​
  ​an​ ​important​ ​operational​ ​question:​ ​due​ ​to​​variable​​load​​demand​​of​​a​​data​​center,​​how​​can​​grid​​operators​
   ​reassess​​power​​resources​​to​​achieve​​reliable​​predictive​​modelling?​​My​​research​ ​focus​​also​​tackles​​the​​same​
    ​challenge​ ​with​ ​advanced​ ​tools,​ ​i.e.​ ​machine-learning-based​ ​electricity​ ​demand​ ​forecasting​ ​and​ ​the​
     ​monitoring​​of​​critical​​energy​ ​infrastructure.​​I​​have​​published​​work​​on​​short-term​​load​​forecasting​​using​​a​
      ​combined​ ​convolutional​ ​neural​ ​networks​ ​and​ ​bidirectional​ ​long​ ​short-term​ ​memory​ ​approach​ ​[1].​ ​The​
​recommendation below draws on that research direction.​

                ​Large​​computing​​facilities​​can​​change​​their​​electricity​​use​​as​​computing​​jobs​​begin,​​end,​​or​​move​
 ​ etween​ ​systems.​ ​Their​ ​cooling​ ​requirements​​can​​also​​change​​with​​ambient​​temperature,​​humidity,​​and​
 b
 ​equipment​ ​activity.​​These​​effects​​may​​occur​​together,​​so​​the​​demand​​that​​is​​plausible​​during​​one​​part​​of​
  ​the​ ​day​ ​may​ ​be​ ​quite​ ​different​ ​a​ ​short​ ​time​ ​later.​ ​Grid​ ​operators​ ​already​ ​update​ ​forecasts​ ​and​ ​make​
   ​operating​ ​decisions​ ​as​ ​conditions​ ​change.​ ​My​ ​recommendation​ ​is​ ​to​ ​examine​ ​whether​ ​these​ ​decisions​
    ​could​ ​be​ ​improved​ ​by​ ​combining​ ​autoregressive,​ ​uncertainty-aware​ ​forecasts​ ​of​​large​​computing​​loads​
     ​with​​a​​method​​that​​explicitly​ ​evaluates​​the​​consequences​​of​​alternative​​reserve​​and​​flexibility​​actions​​over​
​the next several hours.​

​Proposed Approach​
                I​ n​ ​a​ ​limited​ ​research​ ​pilot,​ ​the​ ​system​ ​could​ ​update​ ​its​ ​assessment​ ​every​ ​five​ ​minutes​ ​using​
 ​metered​ ​demand,​ ​weather​ ​and​ ​cooling​ ​information,​ ​the​ ​operating​ ​state​ ​of​ ​available​ ​resources,​ ​and​
  ​information​ ​about​ ​anticipated​ ​changes​ ​in​ ​computing​ ​activity​ ​(if​ ​provided​ ​by​ ​the​ ​data​ ​center).​ ​It​ ​would​
   ​estimate​​a​​range​​of​​possible​​demand​​changes​​over​​the​​next​​hour​​or​​several​​hours,​​including​​sharp​​increases​
    ​and​​decreases,​​rather​​than​​relying​​on​​a​​single​​expected​​value.​​It​​would​​then​​assess​​whether​​the​​reserves​​and​
     ​flexible​ ​resources​ ​available​ ​at​ ​that​ ​moment​ ​are​ ​sufficient​ ​under​ ​several​ ​credible​ ​conditions.​ ​When​ ​the​
      ​assessment​ ​indicates​ ​a​ ​change​ ​in​ ​risk,​ ​it​ ​could​ ​recommend​ ​an​​appropriate​​response,​​such​​as​​maintaining​
       ​additional​ ​reserves,​ ​preparing​ ​available​ ​storage,​ ​or​ ​requesting​ ​a​ ​voluntary​ ​adjustment​ ​to​ ​deferrable​
        ​computing​ ​demand.​ ​The​ ​operator​ ​would​ ​remain​ ​responsible​ ​for​ ​deciding​ ​what​ ​action​ ​is​ ​authorized​ ​and​
​appropriate.​

            ​One​ ​method​ ​worth​​testing​​is​​reinforcement​​learning,​​in​​which​​a​​computer-based​​decision​​system​
l​earns​ ​from​​repeated​​simulated​​situations​​how​​present​​actions​​affect​​later​​conditions.​​This​​may​​be​​useful​
 ​because​ ​a​ ​decision​ ​that​ ​appears​ ​economical​ ​now,​ ​e.g.​ ​using​ ​stored​ ​energy,​ ​can​ ​leave​ ​fewer​ ​options​
  ​available​ ​if​ ​demand​ ​rises​ ​unexpectedly​ ​later.​ ​A​ ​useful​ ​study​ ​should​​compare​​the​​reinforcement​​learning​
   ​based​​gains​​against​​current​​operating​​practices​​and​​a​ ​conventional​​optimization​​method​​that​​also​​updates​
  i​ts​ ​decisions​ ​as​ ​new​ ​information​ ​arrives.​ ​Any​ ​learned​ ​recommendation​ ​would​ ​have​​to​​pass​​independent​
  ​checks​ ​against​ ​operating​ ​limits,​ ​reserve​ ​requirements,​ ​equipment​ ​restrictions,​ ​and​ ​applicable​ ​reliability​
​standards before it could be considered for use.​

​Evaluation and Safeguards​
             ​I​ ​recommend​ ​that​ ​a​ ​pilot​ ​be​ ​evaluated​ ​under​ ​ordinary​ ​operations,​ ​rapid​ ​workload​ ​changes,​
 ​ igh-temperature​​conditions,​​forecast​​errors,​​and​​combinations​​of​​events​​that​​are​​individually​​unlikely​​but​
 h
 ​potentially​ ​serious​ ​together.​ ​The​ ​central​ ​measures​ ​should​ ​be​ ​whether​ ​the​ ​approach​ ​maintains​ ​required​
  ​reliability,​ ​how​ ​often​ ​it​ ​proposes​​actions​​that​​fail​​safety​​checks,​​whether​​it​​improves​​the​​use​​of​​available​
   ​reserves,​ ​and​ ​whether​ ​it​ ​provides​ ​decisions​ ​quickly​ ​enough​ ​to​ ​be​ ​useful.​ ​It​ ​should​ ​also​ ​be​ ​tested​​when​
    ​computing-workload​ ​information​​is​​incomplete​​or​​unavailable.​​A​​method​​that​​performs​​well​​only​​when​​it​
​receives perfect information would have limited operational value.​

              ​The​ ​same​ ​monitoring​ ​process​ ​could​ ​provide​ ​a​ ​secondary​ ​benefit​ ​for​ ​operational​ ​security.​ ​If​
 ​ easured​ ​electricity​ ​use​ ​differs​ ​sharply​ ​from​ ​what​ ​the​ ​facility​ ​and​ ​forecasting​ ​system​ ​expected,​ ​the​
 m
 ​difference​ ​could​ ​prompt​ ​review​ ​of​ ​workload​ ​changes,​ ​cooling-system​​behavior,​​equipment​​faults,​​data​
  ​quality,​ ​or​ ​possible​ ​cybersecurity​ ​concerns.​ ​An​ ​unexpected​ ​load​​pattern​​is​​not,​​by​​itself,​​evidence​​of​​a​
   ​cyber​ ​incident.​ ​Any​ ​exchange​ ​of​ ​computing​ ​or​ ​operational​ ​information​ ​would​ ​require​ ​appropriate​
​security controls and protection of commercially sensitive data.​

​Request for consideration​
               I​ ​ ​encourage​ ​the​ ​Commission​ ​to​ ​consider​ ​whether​ ​voluntary​ ​research​ ​pilots​ ​involving​ ​utilities,​
 ​system​ ​operators,​​and​​large​​computing​​facilities​​could​​establish​​the​​value​​and​​limitations​​of​​this​​approach.​
  ​The​​aim​​is​​not​​to​​replace​​conservative​​planning​​assumptions,​​reduce​​mandatory​​safety​​margins,​​or​​delegate​
   ​control​ ​of​ ​critical​ ​infrastructure​ ​to​ ​an​ ​unverified​ ​model.​ ​It​ ​is​ ​to​ ​determine,​ ​through​ ​measurable​
    ​comparisons,​ ​whether​​continuously​​reassessing​​the​​consequences​​of​​reserve​​and​​flexibility​​decisions​​can​
     ​help​​operators​ ​respond​​to​​the​​unusual​​variability​​of​​large​​AI​​computing​​loads​​while​​preserving​​reliability.​​I​
​appreciate the Commission’s consideration of these comments.​




​ ehmana Younis​
R
​Load Forecasting Researcher​
 ​October 21, 2026​
